questions.q: Why does this lesson say a risk register that is never updated after initial identification is worse than no risk register at all?
options: Because it gives false confidence that risks are still exactly as unmitigated as the day they were first written down
Because unupdated risk registers are illegal under GDPR
Because risk registers automatically expire after 90 days
Because Lesson 6's risks are no longer relevant by Chapter 5
questions.explain: An unupdated register misleads a reader into thinking nothing has changed, when in fact Chapters 2 through 4 actually designed mitigations for each risk — false confidence is worse than an honest 'not yet mitigated' status.

questions.q: What is the critical component that separates a real architecture decision record (ADR) from a plain design summary?
options: The length of the document
Including a diagram in every ADR
Naming the rejected alternatives and the specific reason each was rejected, not just describing what was chosen
Listing every stakeholder who was consulted
questions.explain: A design summary can describe only what was chosen; a real ADR names what wasn't chosen and why, which is what lets a future reader or review board judge whether alternatives were genuinely considered.

questions.q: In ADR-03 (LedgerPoint integration), what alternative was considered and rejected, and why?
options: Multi-org, rejected because of licensing cost
A real-time API integration project, rejected because it would require modernizing core financial infrastructure outside this transformation's scope
Routing LedgerPoint through corporate Okta, rejected for licensing reasons
Full GL replication into Salesforce, rejected because of storage cost
questions.explain: ADR-03 specifically concerns LedgerPoint: the rejected alternative was forcing real-time integration via a modernization project, rejected because that work was outside this transformation's defined scope.

questions.q: What happened to Risk #2's likelihood rating (ownership skew) once the risk register was formalized in Chapter 5?
options: It increased from medium to high, since the risk was never actually addressed
It stayed exactly the same as in Lesson 6, unchanged
It was removed from the register entirely as irrelevant
It was downgraded to low, since queue-based ownership (Lesson 10) is now an actual designed mitigation rather than a placeholder
questions.explain: Because Lesson 10 actually designed the queue-based ownership mitigation, Risk #2's likelihood is downgraded in the formalized register, reflecting that the mitigation is real and designed, not just planned.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say ADRs matter most in preparing for Chapter 6's Architecture Review Board defense?
options: Because an ARB asks not just what was decided but what else was considered and why it wasn't chosen, and a written ADR means that question has a prepared answer instead of an improvised one
Because the ARB only reviews documents, never asks live questions
Because ADRs replace the need for a risk register entirely
Because Chapter 6 is entirely unrelated to the ADRs written in Chapter 5
questions.explain: An ARB specifically probes rejected alternatives and their reasoning; having ADRs already written means the architect has a specific, prepared answer rather than inventing one under live questioning.
